metadata.description: An example graph demonstrating how to use the simulate_rods solver to constrain transforms and stretch a whole biped skeleton.

_notes.text: Apply coloring on the joints. We initialize the joint colors using `default_color` and overwrite the colors of the constrained transforms with `constrained_color`. Finally, display the skeleton in the viewport.

Create the biped skeleton. The `joint_parent_index` and `joint_pivot_matrix` values are hard-coded in two `value` nodes to provide the initial skeleton structure of the biped in a standalone graph. After constructing the skeleton from the raw data, we update the joint transforms so that all transform related geo properties are properly precomputed. Finally, we cache the skeleton to avoid recomputing it since it is not supposed to change every time the graph evaluates.

Translate the toe joint transforms while they are constrained and simulate the biped skeleton as an elastic rod structure. There are a few key points about this setup:

- The `references` port receives the unmodified pivot matrices of the skeleton. This is important because the `transforms` array is modified to translate the joints we intend to drive directly. By supplying the original matrices as `references`, we define the rest pose for the rods from them. The solver compares this rest pose against the simulated `transforms` to compute how each segment is stretched, compressed, or bent.

- `scene_units_in_meter` is set to `0.01` so that 1 scene unit equals 1 cm. The biped skeleton is approximately 175 units tall, and we want it to represent a height of about 1.75 meters in simulation.
You can enable the terminal on this node to view the joint indices in the viewport.

Choose the joints to constrain. In this example, we use two sets: toe joints and passive joints. 

Both sets make the solver inherit the input transforms for those joints. The difference is that we apply a translation to the toe joints before sending them to the solver. This lets us directly drive the toe motion, while the passive joints simply keep their original input transforms.

The toe joints are only constrained for part of the animation. They remain constrained while the current frame is less than `release_frame`. After that, we provide empty indices to the solver, which effectively releases the toe joints from constraint.

You can play with the `release_frame value`, and change which joints are passively constrained by changing the conditions on the `set_passive_indices` node.
